package_info.why_malicious: The package is a typosquat of the legitimate '@typescript-eslint/eslint-plugin' and contains code that drops and persists a trojan executable on the victim's system, enabling further compromise and persistence. It abuses the trust in open source supply chains to deliver malware.

execution_context.trigger: import-time or runtime (when the package is required or executed)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time or runtime, the code writes a disguised executable ('prettier.bat', actually a trojan .exe) to the user's AppData\Roaming directory and copies it to the Windows Startup folder, ensuring it runs on every system boot, enabling persistent malware execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Dropping an executable and persisting it via the Windows Startup folder is a classic malware persistence technique. The use of a misleading .bat extension for an actual executable is deceptive.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate ESLint plugin should not write files to system directories or modify startup settings. It should only provide linting functionality.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate installers may add helper tools to startup, but never from a linter package and never with misleading file types.
key_indicators: Copies file to Windows Startup folder
No legitimate reason for a linter to persist executables

execution_context.trigger: runtime (when the dropped file is executed at system startup)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Binary executable (prettier.bat, actually a .exe) flagged as a trojan and dropper on VirusTotal. Capabilities include accessing Windows registry, exfiltrating files, and installing additional malware.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At system startup, the disguised executable runs with user privileges, potentially accessing sensitive files, registry keys, and establishing network connections to exfiltrate data or download further payloads.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The file is a known trojan/dropper, flagged by VirusTotal, and is delivered under a misleading name and extension.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: No legitimate npm package should install or persist a trojan executable, especially under a misleading filename.
key_indicators: Runs at startup with broad system access

execution_context.trigger: install-time (when the fake prettier package is installed)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
// Pseudocode based on report description
require('child_process').exec('npm install @typescript_eslinter/eslint');
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At install-time, the fake prettier package automatically installs the malicious '@typescript_eslinter/eslint' package as a dependency, ensuring the malware is delivered even if only the prettier typosquat is installed.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Automatically installing another package without user consent is a supply chain attack vector. The intent is to propagate the malware via dependency confusion.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate prettier package should not install unrelated packages or execute arbitrary install commands.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some meta-packages install dependencies, but not in this deceptive, hidden manner.

attack_chain.action: User installs the typosquatted '@typescript_eslinter/eslint' or '@typescript_eslinter/prettier' package, often by mistake or via dependency confusion.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious package is present in the environment.

attack_chain.action: Malicious package executes code to drop a disguised executable ('prettier.bat') into AppData\Roaming and persists it in the Windows Startup folder.
attack_chain.leads_to: Persistence of malware on the system.

attack_chain.action: On system reboot, the trojan executable runs, potentially exfiltrating data, accessing the registry, and installing further malware.
attack_chain.leads_to: System compromise, data exfiltration, and possible further infection.

behavioral_signatures: npm package writing files to AppData\Roaming or Startup folders
Dropping executables with misleading extensions (.bat that is actually .exe)
Persistence via Windows Startup folder from npm package
Automatic installation of additional packages during install
file_indicators: Any .bat file in Startup that is actually a PE executable
network_indicators: Outbound connections from prettier.bat or similar dropped executables
Connections to known C2 or exfiltration endpoints (not specified in report, but typical for such trojans)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor npm package installations for unexpected file writes to AppData\Roaming and Startup folders, especially files with misleading extensions. Flag any npm package that drops executables or modifies startup persistence. Use static and dynamic analysis to detect executables disguised as batch files. Block or alert on installation of known typosquatted packages such as '@typescript_eslinter/eslint' and '@typescript_eslinter/prettier'.
